blocks.1: The house at Haugane where the post office was from 1892 to 1927. From the right: the postmistress Ølla Navdal, her father Mons Haveland and her son Einar Navdal. The postbox hangs by the door. Photo: Unknown
blocks.2: My sources for this are information from the Postal Museum in Oslo (copies of old maps, postal routes etc.) and the local history book.
blocks.3: “The date of establishment is unknown”, writes the Postal Museum, but the place is mentioned as a sub-post office in a list from 1808 of postal stations that were to get a new seal because of a change of king. No other postal stations in Gulen are mentioned there. Eivindvik is written Evenvig in Ytre Sogn, while Leirvik (in Hyllestad) is listed as “Leervig(en) in Evenvig”. This is because Leirvik at that time belonged to Eivindvik parish. The sub-post office here was then in Fonnevika. It was moved over to the mainland in 1892. The post office probably got a room then in the house of Mons Haveland at Haugane (the same house that stands on the holding today). Mons had become postmaster in 1890, the local history says. The post office was first in the cellar but was later moved up into one of the living rooms on the ground floor. Haugane was probably the site of the post office right up until Ansgar Sandal became postmaster in 1927. At Haugane they still have the pigeonholes, the table and the wastepaper basket that were used in the post office there.
blocks.4: “Evindvig” is named on an old postal map from 1785, but whether there was a sub-post office in Eivindvik then, or whether the map only shows the name of the parish, I cannot say. A note to the map (written in “Kiøbenhavn” in 1785) says: “The routes laid out on trial between Bergen and Molde and between Bergen and Stavanger, but not yet most graciously approved, are:”, and then follow the stretches named in our area:
blocks.13: Eivindvik is not named in this proposal for a postal route between Bergen and Molde except on the map, but in those days it was probably more or less only the priest (and sometimes the sheriff) who received post, so if the route did start, I would think the post was brought out here. For a time they tried a sub-post office at Åmdalsvika, so that the post carriers would not have to row out here with the post. This began in Dahl's time, and Klaus Jørgenson (Ytre Midtun) was appointed to handle the post at Åmdalsvika. The local history says that the priests demanded payment from the authorities for the farmhands who had to fetch the priest's post from Åmdalsvika, and this meant that the post was again brought to Eivindvik. The postal arrangement at Åmdalsvika lasted, according to the local history, from 1849 to 1858. Klaus was also the main church cantor, alongside Anders Furnæs.
blocks.14: Klaus had earlier been an itinerant schoolteacher, and it seems that Dahl had picked him out as teacher at the permanent school once the schoolhouse at Undertun was finished. This was, as mentioned before, the first schoolhouse in the whole parish, and it came in 1835. The reason Klaus did not then become teacher there is probably that he had already settled at Åmdalsvika in 1819 (according to the local history).
blocks.15: In 1812 and 1816 the name of the sub-post office in Eivindvik is just “Evenvig”, in 1833 “Evenvig in Ytre Sogn”, later “Eivindvig”, but in the 1889 list of postal stations the name was changed to “Evenvik”, and on 1 May 1901 it was changed again, to “Eivindvik”. Eivindvik used to come under Bergen post office, but from 1 July 1909 it came under Lærdal post office, from 15 January 1928 again under Bergen, from 1 October 1929 again under Lærdal, from 1 July 1953 back to Bergen and then from 1 October 1971 under Førde.
blocks.16: In the period 1785–1858 only 2 postal stations are mentioned in Gulen: Eide, in the route proposal mentioned above, and Eivindvik, in a “Description of Norway's public letter posts” dated Christiania, August 1838. Here “Evenvig” is listed, and in the accompanying timetable route 75 (84), from Bergen to Molde, says:
blocks.33: Route 84 is the return to Bergen. The route took 115 hours from Bergen to Molde and 114 hours on the return, which started from Molde “Tuesday at 9 in the morning.”
blocks.34: About the types of postmark used at Eivindvik sub-post office the Postal Museum writes: “The sub-post office first used 3-ring cancellation stamp no. 62 (c. 1855/6) and was sent a date stamp on 16 December 1858, of the 1-ring type with sans-serif letters.”
blocks.35: About the postmasters I have been given this information: “Those who first handled the post are unknown. A time sheet from 1833/4 is attested by Waage, in 1835 by Alstrup. L. Jørgensen 1 Jan 1849. Parish priest A. Meyer 15 July 1859. Hans E. Lund, temporary 1 April 1878, permanent in 1880. Storekeeper and steamer agent Fredrik Larsen 1 July 1883. Steamer agent Mons M. Haveland 1 April 1893. Sheriff A. Bredvik 5 March 1902. Mons M. Haveland acting from 1 April 1907, permanent 1 Dec 1908. Sigurd M. Haveland 1 Aug 1921. Telephone assistant and steamer agent Ansgar Sandal acting from 1 Nov 1927. Postal driver Nils Arthur Oppedal acting from 1 April 1971. Postal clerk Berit Jorun Haveland Opdal 1 Jan 1977.”
blocks.36: The postmasters' annual pay was 24 speciedaler in 1861, 30 speciedaler in 1866, 180 kroner in 1877, 240 kroner in 1894, 340 kroner in 1901, 500 kroner in 1909, 550 kroner in 1914 and 650 kroner in 1917.
blocks.37: “From 1 July 1917 a temporary cost-of-living supplement of 50% of the then salary was also granted.”
blocks.38: The local historian Karl Gåta Birknes writes in an article in “Gula Tidend” of 21 December 1935 about the postal routes in Sogn. He says there that the postal route between Bergen and Molde started in “the 1786 years”, with a postal station at “Leirvik in Sogn”. “Eivindvik did not become a postal station until 1797, and the parish priest Dressing was the first postmaster”. The article says nothing about where he found this information.
blocks.39: He also writes that Dahl, among others, pressed hard for a cross-connection between the postal route from Oslo to Bergen via Lærdal, Frønningen and Voss and the postal route between Bergen and Molde. Dahl sent a report on this to “Nordre Bergenhus county” on 17 July 1835 and won the authorities over; as early as 1836, by royal decree of 5 May, such a “side post” was started between Leirvik and Frønningen on these two postal routes.
blocks.40: When “Fylkesbaatane” (the county steamship company) started operating in December 1858, they took over carrying the post.
